Q: how can you tell if a replace operator was successful A:

  • Indeed, -replace, the regular-expression-based string replacement operator, does not indicate whether an actual replacement was performed; instead, it always returns a string: either the input string as-is, if no replacement took place, or a modified copy.

  • If no replacements are performed, the very same string instance as the input string is returned, which you can take advantage of for a quick test, whose performance is independent of the size of the input string. That is, you can use [object]::ReferenceEquals() to compare the input string to the -replace return value.

For example:

$100mb_str = 'x' * 50mb

$potentiallyModified_str = $100mb_str -replace 'nomatch', 'y'

# Determine if actual replacements took place.
"Were replacements made?"
-not [object]::ReferenceEquals($100mb_str, $potentiallyModified_str)

Note:

  • The above answers the question as to whether any replacement performed in the strict technical sense; that is, if replacements were performed that happen to result in a string with identical content as the input string, $true is still returned.

    • E.g., 'foo' -replace '^.', 'f' is technically considered a replacement, even though the result is also 'foo'

  • If you're interested in whether the returned string is in effect different, i.e. has different content, you indeed need to examine their contents via string comparison, using [string]::Equals():

    # Determine if replacements took place that *changed the content*:
# Note: Defaults to the 'Ordinal' string-comparison mode, 
#       which is desired here (see below).
"Was the string content modified?"
-not [string]::Equals($100mb_str, $potentiallyModified_str)

    • Note that PowerShell's -eq and -ceq operators can not robustly be used for this test:

      • -eq will ignore differences in case, and while -ceq does not, under the covers it uses the InvariantCulture string-comparison mode (see the System.StringComparison enum), which, along with InvariantCultureIgnoreCase, CurrentCulture, and CurrentCultureIgnoreCase is a mode based on linguistic equivalence rather than on technically identical content; only Ordinal (which [string]::Equals() uses by default) tests for the latter.

      • E.g., 'ü' -ceq "u$([char] 0x308)" is $true, even though the strings clearly differ technically - however, they are considered equal by the rules of Unicode normalization.
        The above operation is equivalent to [string]::Equals('ü', "u$([char] 0x308)", 'InvariantCulture')
        By contrast, [string]::Equals('ü', "u$([char] 0x308)") - which is the same as [string]::Equals('ü', "u$([char] 0x308)", 'Ordinal') - yields $false.

Q: What is the struct tag of anonymous structs in C? A:

For starters you are speaking about unnamed structures that is about structures without tags. Anonymous structures may be only members of another structures.

Two unnamed structures are compatible if they are defined in different translation units and have the same order and types of their members.

The C24 Standard, section "6.2.7 Compatible type and composite type":

Furthermore, two structure, union, or enumerated types declared in separate translation units are compatible in the following cases: — both are declared without tags and they fulfill the preceding requirements;

Two unnamed structures declared in the same translation unit are not compatible.

In the C24 Standard there is a footnote for the section "6.2.7 Compatible type and composite type"

46)A structure, union, or enumerated type without a tag or an incomplete structure, union or enumerated type is not compatible with any other structure, union or enum type declared in the same translation unit.

In my opinion there is a defect in the C24 Standard. Let's assume that two unnamed structures are declared in one translation unit. And in the same time the same two unnamed structures are declared in another translation unit. A question arises: what structures are compatible?

Q: Debug configuration build with OR'ing std::wregex constansts throws an unexpected std::regex_error exception A:

Try using std::regex_constants namespace directly instead of aliases.

re.assign(L"FilE",  
    std::regex_constants::ECMAScript | 
    std::regex_constants::nosubs |
    std::regex_constants::optimize |
    (bCaseSens ? 0 : std::regex_constants::icase)

You use std::regex_constants values when you construct a std::wregex object (or any other std::basic_regex specialization like std::regex) to configure how it should operate.

Q: In Slack, can a bot remove a user from a private channel when it doesn't belong to it? A:

Using the scopes described at https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/conversations.kick/ did the trick for me.

Bot token: channels:managechannels:writegroups:writeim:writempim:write

User token: channels:writegroups:writeim:writempim:write
